title: Data Types and Casting
summary: See the type of every value and convert between types with :: and CAST.
intro: Every value in PostgreSQL has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it. Here you meet the everyday types, ask PostgreSQL what type a value is, and convert text into numbers and dates.

steps.title: Every value has a type
steps.body:
PostgreSQL gives every value a type. These are the ones you will use most:

- `integer`: whole numbers like `42`. Use it for counts.
- `numeric`: exact decimals like `4.2`. Use it for money: it stores every digit exactly, so cents never drift. `numeric(10, 2)` keeps exactly 2 decimal places, so `'19.9'::numeric(10, 2)` prints `19.90`.
- `text`: any string, written in single quotes.
- `boolean`: `true` or `false`. `psql` prints them as `t` and `f`.
- `date`: a calendar day, written `DATE '2025-03-01'` (year, month, day).

To check a type, wrap the value in `pg_typeof()`. It returns the type's name:

```sql
SELECT pg_typeof(42) AS whole_type;
```

One gotcha: a bare quoted string has no type yet. PostgreSQL waits to see how you use it, so `pg_typeof('hello')` says `unknown`. The next part shows how to give it a type on purpose.

This lesson needs no tables. Every program works on values you type straight into the `SELECT`.

example.title: Four types and how they print
example.prompt: Show the type of a whole number, a decimal, a boolean, and a date, then show how a boolean and a date print.
example.code:
SELECT pg_typeof(42) AS whole_type, pg_typeof(4.2) AS decimal_type, pg_typeof(true) AS bool_type, pg_typeof(DATE '2025-03-01') AS date_type;
SELECT true AS yes, false AS no, DATE '2025-03-01' AS day;
example.output:
whole_type | decimal_type | bool_type | date_type
------------+--------------+-----------+-----------
 integer    | numeric      | boolean   | date
(1 row)

 yes | no |    day
-----+----+------------
 t   | f  | 2025-03-01
(1 row)
example.explanation: `42` has no decimal point, so it is an `integer`. `4.2` has one, so it is `numeric`. The first row shows each type's name. In the second statement the values themselves come back: `psql` prints `true` as `t`, `false` as `f`, and a date as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

practice.title: Types of an order
practice.prompt:
Show the types of four values from an order, then show how its flags and deadline print.

1. In one `SELECT`, show `pg_typeof()` of `7` as `count_type`, of `0.5` as `price_type`, of `false` as `flag_type`, and of `DATE '1999-12-31'` as `day_type`.
2. In a second `SELECT`, show `false` as `paid`, `true` as `shipped`, and `DATE '1999-12-31'` as `deadline`.

Expected output:

```text
 count_type | price_type | flag_type | day_type
------------+------------+-----------+----------
 integer    | numeric    | boolean   | date
(1 row)

 paid | shipped |  deadline
------+---------+------------
 f    | t       | 1999-12-31
(1 row)
```
practice.solution:
SELECT pg_typeof(7) AS count_type, pg_typeof(0.5) AS price_type, pg_typeof(false) AS flag_type, pg_typeof(DATE '1999-12-31') AS day_type;
SELECT false AS paid, true AS shipped, DATE '1999-12-31' AS deadline;

tests.output:
count_type | price_type | flag_type | day_type
------------+------------+-----------+----------
 integer    | numeric    | boolean   | date
(1 row)

 paid | shipped |  deadline
------+---------+------------
 f    | t       | 1999-12-31
(1 row)

hints: Each column is `pg_typeof(value) AS name`, separated by commas.
Write the date as `DATE '1999-12-31'` in both statements.

steps.title: Converting with :: and CAST
steps.body:
A cast converts a value to another type. PostgreSQL has two spellings that do the same thing:

```sql
SELECT '42'::integer AS short_form, CAST('42' AS integer) AS long_form;
```

`CAST(value AS type)` is standard SQL and works in every database. `value::type` is PostgreSQL's shorter form, and the one you will see most. Casting is how text becomes a number you can add, or a date you can do math on:

- `'19.99'::numeric` gives an exact decimal.
- `'2025-03-01'::date` gives a date.
- `date + integer` adds that many days, and `date - integer` subtracts them. The result is still a date.

The text has to look like the type. A cast that cannot work stops the program with an error:

```text
ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "abc"
```

Even `'4.5'::integer` fails, because the text `4.5` is not a whole number, and `'2025-02-30'::date` fails because February has no 30th. Casting a number instead of text rounds it: `4.5::integer` gives `5`. Try `SELECT 'abc'::integer;` in the editor to see the error yourself, then remove it.

example.title: Totals from text
example.prompt: Turn three text values into an integer, a decimal, and a date, and do math on each.
example.code: SELECT '42'::integer + 8 AS total, CAST('19.99' AS numeric) * 2 AS double_price, '2025-03-01'::date + 30 AS due;
example.explanation: `::` binds tighter than math, so `'42'::integer` turns the text into the number 42 first, and adding 8 gives 50. `CAST('19.99' AS numeric)` is an exact decimal, so doubling it gives exactly 39.98. `'2025-03-01'::date + 30` moves 30 days forward and lands on March 31.

practice.title: Order math from text
practice.prompt:
In one `SELECT`, cast three text values and do math on each, giving every column an alias.

1. Cast `'15'` to `integer` with `::` and multiply it by 3, as `tripled`.
2. Use `CAST` to turn `'4.75'` into `numeric` and add `0.25`, as `total`. It prints as `5.00` because `numeric` keeps the two decimal places of its inputs.
3. Cast `'2025-12-25'` to `date` with `::` and subtract 7 days, as `week_before`.

Expected output:

```text
 tripled | total | week_before
---------+-------+-------------
      45 |  5.00 | 2025-12-18
(1 row)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: cast the text '15', '4.75', and '2025-12-25', then do the math
SELECT '15' AS tripled;
practice.solution: SELECT '15'::integer * 3 AS tripled, CAST('4.75' AS numeric) + 0.25 AS total, '2025-12-25'::date - 7 AS week_before;
hints: Cast first, then do the math: `'7'::integer * 2` turns the text into 7 before multiplying.
Inside `CAST` the type goes after `AS`, like `CAST('1.50' AS numeric)`.
Subtracting an integer from a date moves it back that many days.

recap:
- Common types: `integer`, `numeric`, `text`, `boolean` (printed `t` and `f`), and `date` (written `DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD'`).
- `pg_typeof(value)` names a value's type. A bare quoted string is `unknown` until it is used.
- `value::type` and `CAST(value AS type)` both convert a value.
- `date + integer` and `date - integer` move by days.
- A cast that cannot work, like `'abc'::integer`, is an error.
